# **AquaSentinel Real-Time Data and Detection Architecture**

## **1\. Dataset Audit and Exact Data Contract**

An exhaustive audit of the BattLeDIM L-Town benchmark dataset establishes the foundational parameters for the AquaSentinel streaming architecture1. The dataset provides a rigorous simulation of a municipal water distribution network (WDN), encompassing 782 junction nodes and 905 pipe segments spanning approximately 42.6 kilometers of infrastructure3. The network is divided into three primary district metered areas (DMAs)—Area A, Area B, and Area C—which exhibit distinct demand profiles and hydraulic behaviors5. To ensure realistic hydraulic behavior during simulation, the data generation engine leverages the EPANET 2.2 and WNTR frameworks, specifically utilizing pressure-dependent demand (PDD) mechanics4. Under this paradigm, node demand is modulated by local pressure. The exact parameters governing this relationship in the L-Town dataset are a minimum pressure ![][image1] meters (below which demand is zero), a nominal pressure ![][image2] meters (above which full demand is met), and an exponent ![][image3]4.  
The minimum viable dataset required to implement and evaluate the core detector consists of the historical 2018 records (designated for baseline model fitting and parameter tuning) and the 2019 records (strictly reserved for sequential evaluation)5. The critical files include Pressures.csv (recording high-frequency telemetry from 33 pressure sensors), Flows.csv (recording total inflow telemetry from three flow meters), and Leakages.csv (containing the authoritative ground-truth event labels)3. All sensor measurements are sampled at a strict five-minute interval5.  
A known vulnerability in processing high-frequency time-series datasets within Python involves timestamp parsing, particularly the mismanagement of naive versus timezone-aware datetime objects. When utilizing Pandas to read chronological data, mixed timezone offsets or daylight saving transitions frequently trigger ValueError exceptions or silently corrupt the temporal sequence9. To guarantee chronological integrity, all timestamps must be parsed directly into Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) utilizing strict format strings and functions equivalent to pandas.to\_datetime(..., utc=True)9.  
The ground-truth leakage data introduces critical semantic nuances that dictate evaluation design. The dataset explicitly models physical leaks as localized emitters governed by an emitter coefficient (![][image4]) and an exponent of 0.5, simulating fluid discharging through an orifice12. The labels define the exact physical onset time, the peak time, and the maximum diameter of the simulated burst4. The algorithmic alert generation must be evaluated against the physical onset time, not the repair time, as the primary utility objective is minimizing the duration of the unseen leak4.  
The finalized data contract defining the inputs, constraints, and validation rules for the streaming ingestion pipeline is established below.

| Field Name | Data Type | Units | Validation Rules | Missing-Data Handling Strategy |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| timestamp | datetime64\[ns, UTC\] | ISO8601 | Strictly monotonic, regular 5-minute intervals. | Forward fill up to 3 intervals; flag thereafter. |
| sensor\_id | string | N/A | Must explicitly exist in the predefined L-Town sensor topology. | Reject and log anomalous records. |
| value | float32 | L/s (Flow), m (Pressure) | Non-negative; must fall within plausible physical limits for the network. | Hold last valid state; suspend statistical anomaly decay. |
| sensor\_type | string | N/A | Must be classified as 'FLOW', 'PRESSURE', or 'AMR'. | Reject unclassified records. |
| event\_label | boolean | N/A | Exists only in historical data. True if within ![][image5]. | Assume False if not explicitly provided during historical training. |

## **2\. Processing Pipeline Diagram**

The processing pipeline is architected to emulate a strict real-time Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) environment. Vectorized, whole-dataset operations (such as pandas.DataFrame.rolling) are fundamentally incompatible with this requirement, as they process data eagerly and risk lookahead bias14. Instead, the architecture utilizes an asynchronous, generator-driven design that guarantees sequential, memory-efficient processing of individual observations15. The pipeline executes the following nine stages sequentially for each discrete timestamp:

> 1. **Read and validate historical data:** The system initializes by loading the historical 2018 SCADA arrays into an optimized asyncio.Queue15. A zero-copy memory architecture, leveraging Numpy arrays or PyArrow tables, is utilized to prevent the massive computational overhead associated with instantiating individual Pandas Series objects for every row17.  
> 2. **Fit the historical baseline:** A robust time-of-day and day-of-week demand baseline is calculated utilizing the 2018 flow telemetry. This involves extracting diurnal consumption patterns using Fourier series decomposition or moving medians5.  
> 3. **Estimate residual variability using an appropriate historical period:** The variance (![][image6]) of the residuals—defined as the difference between historical observations and the fitted baseline—is calculated. This variance establishes the normalization parameters required for the statistical detector.  
> 4. **Normalize incoming observations:** As a new observation arrives sequentially at time ![][image7], the expected baseline value is subtracted to compute the raw residual. This value is then divided by the historical standard deviation to yield the normalized residual, ![][image8].  
> 5. **Update the CUSUM state for each channel:** The normalized residual is ingested by a stateful Cumulative Sum (CUSUM) engine. The internal state, ![][image9], is updated recursively based exclusively on the prior state ![][image10], the current normalized residual ![][image8], and a predefined slack parameter ![][image11]20.  
> 6. **Apply calibrated alert thresholds:** The current CUSUM state ![][image9] is evaluated against a static decision interval threshold, ![][image12]. An alert flag is triggered immediately for timestamp ![][image7] if the threshold is breached22.  
> 7. **Group repeated alerts into incidents:** Persistent leakage triggers continuous or rapidly oscillating threshold violations. An Incident Manager applies temporal clustering to group localized alerts into a single, cohesive incident state, defining an inferred onset and ongoing duration.  
> 8. **Record evidence and evaluation outputs:** The raw flow value, normalized residual, current CUSUM trajectory, threshold status, and active incident identifiers are appended to a pre-allocated output buffer for performance evaluation.  
> 9. **Publish the updated status to the dashboard:** The updated system state is asynchronously yielded to the presentation or user interface layer, fulfilling the requirement for simulated live-telemetry delivery.

| Processing Stage | Input Dependencies | Component State Requirements | Error Handling |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Ingestion** | Raw CSV or Data Stream | Stateless | Drop malformed rows; forward-fill brief missing gaps. |
| **Normalization** | Current observation, Frozen baseline | Frozen (![][image13], ![][image14]) parameters | Suspend calculation if data exceeds 15-minute gap. |
| **CUSUM Inference** | Normalized residual (![][image8]) | Stateful (![][image10]) | Hold previous state ![][image10] during data outages. |
| **Alert Generation** | **![][image9]**, Threshold (![][image12]) | Stateless | Fail-safe: default to 'no alert' on computational error. |
| **Incident Management** | Current alert flag, Time gap | Stateful (Active Incident ID) | Close active incidents if timestamp jumps significantly. |

## **3\. Prevent Data Leakage**

Preventing information leakage—the inadvertent assimilation of future information into present predictions—is the most critical requirement for validating the AquaSentinel architecture. The benchmark explicitly provides a structured chronological split: the 2018 dataset serves as the historical training environment, and the 2019 dataset serves as the untouched evaluation environment4.  
The baseline models must be fitted exclusively using the 2018 dataset. During this phase, it is vital to identify and handle leak-active intervals. Any interval annotated as an active leak in the 2018 Leakages.csv metadata must be forcibly masked (e.g., converted to NaN) prior to calculating the diurnal flow baselines. Failure to mask these events allows the baseline model to artificially inflate, effectively learning the elevated demand caused by the leak. The historical residual variability (![][image14]) must also be computed strictly on this leak-masked subset of the 2018 data.  
Detector thresholds (![][image12]) and slack parameters (![][image11]) are tuned via grid search exclusively over the 2018 dataset. A simulated sequential evaluation is executed on the historical data to optimize these parameters, maximizing the detection of known 2018 events while constraining the false alarm rate to an acceptable utility tolerance. Once optimal values are identified, all detector parameters—the baseline profiles, the residual standard deviation ![][image14], the slack ![][image11], and the threshold ![][image12]—are strictly frozen.  
During the final evaluation over the 2019 dataset, the system processes the data sequentially, moving strictly forward in time. To ensure absolute chronological integrity, the testing script must be implemented as a state machine. The system maintains an internal buffer representing only the past ![][image15] observations, actively overwriting older data to prevent retrospective analysis.  
If online baseline updating is utilized to adapt to seasonal demand drift or expanding consumer bases, the updating mechanism must only incorporate data up to time ![][image16]. Crucially, this online update requires robust state gating: if the detection engine currently suspects an anomaly (i.e., the CUSUM state is elevated above zero), the online baseline update must be suspended. If the baseline is allowed to update during a leak, the expected mean will gradually rise to match the leak volume, causing the residual to decay back to zero and masking the ongoing physical fault.  
When converting continuous time-series predictions into discrete event-level results, a rigorous label-matching rule is employed. An algorithmic alert triggered at time ![][image17] is successfully matched to a physical leak with onset ![][image18] if, and only if, ![][image17] falls within the strict chronological window ![][image19], where ![][image20] represents the maximum allowable detection delay threshold (e.g., 7 days). Any alerts occurring outside predefined active leak windows are classified and penalized as false positive alarms.

## **4\. Research the Detection-Engine Trade-offs**

The core functionality of the AquaSentinel architecture relies entirely on the selection and calibration of an optimal statistical detection engine. The fundamental premise of leak detection in WDNs is that a physical failure manifests as a persistent increase in fluid flow above the expected diurnal demand22. However, flow residuals are inherently noisy due to stochastic, unmetered consumer activity. The following frameworks present mathematically distinct trade-offs for identifying underlying shifts amidst this noise.  
**Static Thresholds:** A static threshold applied directly to the raw flow telemetry assumes that a leak will uniformly push the total volumetric flow above a historical maximum. This approach is highly vulnerable to diurnal demand fluctuations; a severe pipe burst occurring during a low-demand night period may not exceed the regular daytime peak flow, resulting in an undetected fault (a false negative). Static thresholds are statistically naive and are included strictly as a trivial baseline comparator.  
**Baseline-Only Deviations:** This approach subtracts the modeled baseline demand from the raw flow and applies a static threshold directly to the resulting instantaneous residual. While this isolates the anomaly from diurnal patterns, the instantaneous residual remains highly susceptible to stochastic noise. A sudden, legitimate burst of localized consumption (e.g., municipal hydrant flushing or industrial draw) will trigger an immediate false alarm. To suppress excessive false positives, the threshold must be set exceptionally high, which inherently blinds the system to incipient, slowly growing leaks24.  
**One-Sided CUSUM:** The one-sided Cumulative Sum (CUSUM) algorithm is mathematically designed to detect small, persistent shifts in the mean of a monitored process22. The upper one-sided CUSUM state, utilized for detecting volumetric flow increases, is defined recursively as ![][image21], where ![][image8] is the normalized residual and ![][image11] is the slack parameter20. The parameter ![][image11] functions as a high-pass statistical filter, allowing the system to ignore minor fluctuations below the expected shift magnitude25. Because CUSUM accumulates evidence geometrically over time, it provides superior sensitivity to small, sustained leaks compared to instantaneous deviation checks. However, CUSUM strictly detects persistent statistical changes; it cannot definitively prove physical causation. A sustained change in underlying consumer demand or a persistent positive sensor drift will also trigger the detector26.  
**EWMA (Exponentially Weighted Moving Average):** The EWMA control chart tracks the moving average of the process by applying exponentially decreasing weights to older observations28. While EWMA is highly effective for smoothing autocorrelated data, literature demonstrates that CUSUM exploits temporal structure more effectively for sudden, persistent mean shifts20. EWMA charts frequently generate excessive false alarms in highly volatile flow environments unless they are heavily smoothed, a modification that inherently and unacceptably delays physical detection29.  
**SPRT (Sequential Probability Ratio Test):** The SPRT relies on calculating the log-likelihood ratio between a null hypothesis (no leak) and an alternative hypothesis (leak)30. The test statistic ![][image22] accumulates evidence until it crosses either an upper boundary ![][image23] (accepting the leak hypothesis) or a lower boundary ![][image24] (accepting the null hypothesis)31. While SPRT achieves asymptotic optimality for minimizing detection delay when pre-change and post-change distributions are fully known13, its critical flaw in water leak detection is the strict requirement to define the specific post-change parameter (![][image25]). Because leak magnitudes vary wildly based on orifice size and pressure, a mismatched ![][image25] severely degrades SPRT performance. The CUSUM chart circumvents this by effectively operating as a continuous sequence of SPRTs with a reflecting boundary at zero, making it infinitely more flexible for generalized shift detection30. Consequently, SPRT is theoretically robust but practically cumbersome for variable leak profiles.  
**Pressure Corroboration (Additional Evidence Signal):** Relying solely on flow metrics leaves the detection system vulnerable to false alarms generated by legitimate demand increases. Integrating pressure corroboration introduces a vital physical constraint grounded in fluid dynamics. According to the Hazen-Williams equation, head loss (![][image26]) in a pipe is proportional to flow velocity: ![][image27]35. Therefore, a genuine leak increases local flow while simultaneously depressing local pressure downstream due to the increased frictional energy loss22. If the flow CUSUM triggers a high-flow alert, the system can interrogate the local pressure residuals. If the pressure residuals demonstrate a concurrent negative CUSUM drift, the confidence that the event is a physical leak—rather than sensor drift or a localized demand surge—increases significantly22. This corroboration adds algorithmic complexity but substantially improves precision.  
*Recommendation:* The primary candidate of a time-of-day baseline followed by a one-sided CUSUM on flow residuals is fully justified and selected for implementation. The CUSUM slack parameter ![][image11] provides the necessary statistical insensitivity to acceptable demand variations, while the accumulation mechanism ensures the eventual detection of incipient leaks. Pressure corroboration must be implemented as a secondary validation gate to suppress false alarms generated by demand anomalies.

## **5\. Define Evaluation and Alert-State Architecture**

To objectively compare the deployed detection pipelines, a rigorous evaluation architecture is necessitated. The primary statistical metric governing the performance of control charts is the Average Run Length (ARL), where ![][image28] denotes the expected number of samples processed before a false alarm is triggered, and ![][image29] denotes the expected samples required to detect a true underlying shift38. Siegmund's approximation provides a theoretical basis for this: ![][image30], where ![][image31] and ![][image32]40. In an applied setting, these theoretical properties translate into the following operational metrics:  
**Event-Level Recall:** Recall is calculated as the ratio of successfully detected physical leaks to the total number of physical leaks present in the ground-truth dataset42. An event is considered successfully detected if an incident state is triggered within the active temporal window of the leak.  
**Precision:** Precision measures the proportion of algorithmic alerts that correspond to true physical leaks, calculated as ![][image33]13. High precision indicates that utility crews will not be dispatched to investigate false alarms.  
**False Alarms per Simulated Network Month:** Given the severe operational and economic burden of deploying excavation and repair crews, the absolute frequency of false alarms must be tracked. This is computed by dividing the total number of false positive incidents by the duration of the evaluation period in months.  
**Detection Delay:** For successfully detected events, the detection delay quantifies the temporal difference between the physical ground-truth onset time and the exact timestamp of the first algorithmic alert13.  
**Simulated Leakage Volume Before Alert:** Where the dataset provides continuous simulated leakage flow rates, the volumetric water loss prior to detection is computed by integrating the leak flow rate from ![][image18] to ![][image34]. In the EPANET model, leak flow follows the emitter equation ![][image35], where ![][image36]12. Minimizing this integral serves as the primary economic optimization metric.  
**Event Grouping and Incident States:** The system must gracefully manage continuing events to avoid disproportionately penalizing the algorithm for multiple discrete alerts tied to a single physical leak. The CUSUM state will naturally remain elevated or oscillate near the threshold during a continuing leak. The Incident Manager groups contiguous threshold violations into a single incident block if they occur within a predefined temporal gap (![][image37]).  
An incident enters the **Suspected** state upon the initial threshold crossing. For the Minimum Viable Product (MVP), if the alert is subsequently corroborated via pressure metrics, it is escalated to the **Acknowledged** state. If the CUSUM state drops back to zero and remains there for a predefined reset window (e.g., 24 hours), the incident is formally marked **Resolved**. Any new threshold crossings occurring after the reset window are treated as novel, independent incidents. The system must strictly avoid claims of calibrated probabilistic confidence unless probability calibration mechanisms have been empirically demonstrated.

## **6\. Define Real-Time Behaviour**

The hackathon constraints strictly dictate that the system must replay timestamped data chronologically, guaranteeing zero lookahead to simulate true real-time behavior.  
The most robust mechanism for maintaining detector state and delivering updates relies on leveraging Python's asynchronous capabilities coupled with zero-copy memory operations. An asyncio.Queue serves as the primary asynchronous conduit between the data ingestion layer and the statistical inference engine15. The data reader reads a chunk of telemetry and yields one row at a time to the queue. The detection engine awaits the queue, pulls the single vector, computes the baseline residual, updates the scalar CUSUM state, and yields the result to an output stream44.  
To explicitly distinguish data replay from a live SCADA connection, the system utilizes replay-speed controls. A sleep modifier mechanism is implemented within the asynchronous event loop using await asyncio.sleep(real\_interval / speed\_factor). If speed\_factor is set to 1, the system replays in true real-time (waiting exactly 5 minutes between readings). If speed\_factor is set to 1000, the system processes historical data rapidly while maintaining the exact blocking logic and operational constraints of a live socket connection.  
Latency is precisely measured by calculating the microsecond delta between the time the data vector is yielded to the internal queue and the time the final detection result is published to the dashboard interface. For optimal performance under these constraints, the internal state histories should be maintained using pre-allocated Numpy arrays or memoryview objects, circumventing the severe memory fragmentation and overhead associated with instantiating new Pandas Series objects on a row-by-row basis18.

## **7\. Validate Technical Recommendations**

All technical methodologies proposed within this architecture are strictly grounded in established hydraulic research, statistical process control literature, and official documentation:

* **Dataset Schema & Hydraulics:** The BattLeDIM L-Town dataset (Zenodo Record 4017659\) strictly adheres to the topological and sensor layout detailed, with 5-minute sampling intervals and leakage defined via pressure-dependent emitter coefficients governed by the FAVAD (Fixed and Variable Area Discharges) principles embedded in WNTR1.  
* **CUSUM Mechanics:** The fundamental algorithms for the tabular one-sided CUSUM, including the critical reliance on the slack parameter ![][image11] and the decision threshold ![][image12], are derived directly from canonical statistical process control methodologies established by Page and Siegmund20.  
* **Sequential Probability Ratio Test (SPRT):** The limitations of SPRT regarding the unknown post-change magnitude (![][image25]) and the mathematical relationship positioning CUSUM as a sequence of SPRTs are established in sequential detection theory30.  
* **Zero-Copy Streaming:** The recommendation to utilize Numpy over row-by-row Pandas execution for streaming performance is validated by software engineering benchmarking involving the Python Buffer Protocol, highlighting the architectural limitations of eager evaluation frameworks14.  
* **Timezone Parsing:** The absolute necessity of utilizing utc=True during pandas.to\_datetime execution to resolve mixed offsets and prevent naive-datetime collision is explicitly documented in the official Pandas API specifications9.

*Note: Performance benchmarks, exact precision/recall figures, and false-alarm rates for the specific AquaSentinel parameter tuning must still be empirically measured by the engineering team on the 2018 dataset prior to final evaluation. No performance metrics are fabricated herein.*

## **8\. Minimal Module/Component Boundaries**

The software architecture is modularized to ensure maximum testability, rapid implementation, and clear separation of concerns within the five-hour hackathon constraint:

* StreamIngestor: Responsible for parsing CSV files, handling ISO8601 timezone conversions to UTC, and yielding data row-by-row via an asyncio.Queue.  
* BaselineEngine: Maintains the historical time-of-day flow and pressure profiles. Accepts a timestamp and returns the expected normal vector.  
* CUSUMDetector: A stateful class initialized with optimized ![][image11] and ![][image12] parameters. Receives normalized residuals, updates internal geometric states utilizing Numpy, and returns boolean alert flags.  
* IncidentManager: Tracks active alerts, applies temporal grouping logic, and manages the state machine transitions (Suspected \-\> Acknowledged \-\> Resolved).  
* Evaluator: Consumes the final ground-truth labels and generated incident logs to calculate Recall, Precision, False Alarm Rate, and Detection Delay.

## **9\. Tests That Must Pass Before the Dashboard is Trusted**

Before the pipeline is authorized for final 2019 execution, it must programmatically pass the following automated unit tests:

> 1. **Monotonicity Test:** The StreamIngestor must assert that timestamp\[t\] \> timestamp\[t-1\]. Any violation of strict chronology triggers an immediate pipeline halt.  
> 2. **Zero-Lookahead Test:** A synthesized dummy dataset featuring an obvious step-change at index ![][image15] is processed. The state of the CUSUMDetector at index ![][image38] must identically equal 0, proving no future data contaminated the present calculation.  
> 3. **Missing Data Decay Test:** If three consecutive NaN values are fed to the pipeline, the CUSUM state must freeze at its previous value, proving that artificial zero-residuals generated by missing data are not pulling the cumulative sum downward.  
> 4. **Incident Grouping Test:** A sequence of rapidly alternating alert flags (e.g., 1, 1, 0, 1, 1\) over a two-hour window must result in the generation of exactly one Incident ID, validating the temporal clustering logic.

## **10\. Failure Conditions and Fallbacks**

The streaming architecture must remain resilient to edge cases and hardware failures typical of physical SCADA sensor networks:

* **Sensor Dropouts:** If a flow sensor fails entirely, the pipeline falls back to imputing data based on the last known valid value, but only up to a maximum limit of 15 minutes (3 intervals). Beyond 15 minutes, statistical anomaly detection for that specific network channel is suspended to prevent wild CUSUM divergence.  
* **Persistent Sensor Drift:** If a sensor physically decalibrates, shifting the baseline permanently without a physical leak, the CUSUM will trigger continuously. To mitigate this, if an incident remains in the 'Suspected' state for over 14 days without secondary physical corroboration (e.g., concurrent pressure drops), the system explicitly flags the sensor for "Calibration Review" and initiates an automatic online baseline update to absorb the new mean, resetting the CUSUM to zero.

## **11\. Explicit Assumptions and Evidence Gaps**

* **Assumption:** It is assumed that the physical onset time provided in the 2018/2019 dataset labels corresponds directly to the immediate initiation of a detectable flow deviation at the DMA inlet4.  
* **Assumption:** The architecture assumes that physical leaks inherently cause an increase in total flow at the DMA inlet, driven by the pressure-dependent emitter equations utilized in the simulation12.  
* **Evidence Gap:** The currently available flow and pressure measurements cannot definitively distinguish a genuine subterranean pipe burst from a sudden, persistent authorized demand change (e.g., a municipality opening a new unmetered connection or fire hydrant). The system successfully detects statistical anomalies; human-in-the-loop verification remains an absolute necessity to confirm physical causation.

## **12\. Step-by-Step Implementation Order**

To deliver a functionally robust system within the five-hour constraint, execution must follow a strict chronological prioritization:

* **Hour 1: Data Infrastructure.** Build the StreamIngestor leveraging Pandas for initial bulk disk reads and an asynchronous Python generator for row-by-row yielding. Implement strict timezone handling utilizing utc=True.  
* **Hour 2: Baseline Model.** Calculate the median time-of-day flow profiles on the 2018 data. Programmatically mask all 2018 known leak periods using the metadata prior to calculating the mean and standard deviation (![][image14]).  
* **Hour 3: Core Detectors.** Implement the stateful CUSUMDetector utilizing Numpy arrays for state tracking. Implement the StaticThreshold baseline comparator. Execute both models against the data stream.  
* **Hour 4: State Management & Metrics.** Build the IncidentManager to apply temporal clustering to contiguous alerts. Write the Evaluator module to cross-reference incident times against the 2019 ground-truth labels and calculate Precision, Recall, and Detection Delay.  
* **Hour 5: Refinement & Validation.** Implement pressure corroboration logic based on fluid dynamic constraints. Fine-tune the ![][image11] and ![][image12] parameters utilizing grid search over a masked subset of the 2018 data. Finalize the dashboard output stream and execute the unit test suite.

### **Go/No-Go Checklist for the Detection Pipeline**

* \[ \] Data ingestion explicitly parses timestamps to UTC to avoid timezone/offset drift.  
* \[ \] 2018 evaluation leaks are completely masked (NaN) during the baseline training phase.  
* \[ \] The streaming loop mathematically guarantees zero-lookahead (only data ![][image39] is accessible).  
* \[ \] CUSUM state updates correctly freeze upon encountering predefined missing data limits.  
* \[ \] Incident grouping logic successfully merges oscillating CUSUM alerts into a single continuous physical event.  
* \[ \] Evaluation metric calculations strictly penalize out-of-window alerts as false positives.  
* \[ \] Parameter tuning (![][image11], ![][image12]) is completed solely on 2018 data and explicitly frozen for 2019 evaluation.
